paras: The lynching of King and Joe Richmond took place on August 29, 1915, in Sulphur Springs, Texas, when a crowd burned King Richmond, a wounded Black man, at the stake in Buford Park together with the body of his brother Joe, whom a posse had killed hours earlier. The brothers had been accused of killing Deputy Sheriff Nathan A. Flippen and wounding Sheriff J. B. Butler of Hopkins County that morning. Wire reports of a crowd of thousands and a burning moved from the town square to a park ran nationally, and several Black weeklies answered with editorials.

According to the Associated Press, Butler and Flippen set out that Sunday morning to arrest King Richmond on a 'minor charge' at a Black settlement about nine miles south of Sulphur Springs. In the officers' version, both brothers opened fire 'suddenly and unexpectedly', killing Flippen and leaving Butler shot and beaten, his skull fractured. The Bryan Daily Eagle, a Texas paper, said instead that the two had already been arrested and that one drew a pistol while being searched.

Posses of several hundred men from Hopkins and the neighboring counties of Hunt, Fannin and Franklin searched the countryside. That afternoon they surrounded the brothers in a wood or thicket, and in the fight that followed Joe Richmond was killed and King seriously wounded; none of the posse was hurt. One dispatch says the peace officers in the search were 'in the minority in the posse and were unable to cope with the mob spirit.'

A leased-wire dispatch says fifteen hundred men dragged the wounded man and his brother's body to town, where about five thousand more people joined them. Hundreds demanded a burning in the public square, while 'influential men' urged that the law take its course and officials warned that it would ruin the city's good name. Under the compromise, the wounded man and the 'shot-torn body' were taken to Buford Park on the outskirts and burned at the stake at about 5 p.m. A Globe-Democrat account adds that the pyre was made of dry-goods boxes soaked with oil, that dozens of revolvers were emptied into the fire, and that a woman fired into the flames.
Sulphur Springs was reported quiet the next morning, and no arrest, inquest or grand jury inquiry, nor any later report on Sheriff Butler, appears in the coverage.

White papers from Connecticut to Hawaii carried the Associated Press story on August 30 and 31 under headlines such as 'BURNED AT STAKE' and 'Infuriated Mob Burns Bodies of Negroes at Stake'. The wire lead framed the burning as 'Revenge for the slaying of a deputy sheriff' and gave the officers' account as fact, and the Albuquerque Morning Journal headlined the brothers 'NEGRO DESPERADOES'. White comment was rare, though the Wheeling Intelligencer wrote sarcastically that a Texas mob 'inspired by the "best citizens" of Georgia' had 'vindicated the law'.

Black weeklies took up the story in early September, usually reprinting the wire text inside their own commentary. The New York Age said it did not know the circumstances of the shooting but that 'Negroes in Texas do not go around shooting sheriffs and deputy sheriffs for nothing', and closed with 'LET THE NATION WAKE UP!' The Metropolis Weekly Gazette added 'Shame on so called christianed and civilized America!' to its reprint, and the Richmond Planet devoted an editorial to the burning.

The Cleveland Gazette twice ran the AP item, which called the burning yesterday's 'holiday', as 'Texas' and the south's answer' to a Tribune editorial. The Kansas City Plaindealer's correspondent wrote that the town had 'roasted two Negroes' who 'were not charged with rape, either', while the Tulsa Star printed the wire account without comment.

Most wire texts say Joe was killed by the posse and King burned alive, but the Richmond Times-Dispatch reversed the brothers. The earliest short AP text and the Globe-Democrat account describe both men as burned to death, while the fuller reports agree one was already dead.

reader.title: Lynching of King and Joe Richmond
bases: After a posse killed one brother in a gunfight, a crowd burned the wounded survivor at the stake with the body in a city park (A1, A3, A11).

A crowd put at 1,500 to 5,000 burned a wounded, captured man at the stake without any legal process, as 'revenge' for the killing of a deputy sheriff (A1, A3, A20); his brother had been killed by the posse beforehand, and his body was burned with him (A7, A11).

The Associated Press reports (A1, A6, A11) and a separately worded leased-wire dispatch (A3) agree on the posse fight, the capture and the burning in Buford Park, though they differ on details such as which brother died (A9).

accounts.label: Leased-wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Officers tried to arrest the brothers on a minor charge; 1,500 men dragged the wounded man and the body to town, where 5,000 joined them, and officials steered the burning away from the square to protect the city's good name.

accounts.label: Black editorial voice
accounts.gist: The New York Age said it did not know what led to the shooting but that Black Texans did not shoot officers 'for nothing', and called the crowd a pack of bloodhounds.

framing.detail: AP stories led with 'Revenge for the slaying of a deputy sheriff' and gave the officers' account as fact, under headlines like 'Infuriated Mob Burns Bodies of Negroes at Stake'.
The Albuquerque Morning Journal headlined the victims 'NEGRO DESPERADOES', while the Texas Bryan Eagle's follow-up called the burning a 'Horrible Spectacle'.
The Wheeling Intelligencer said sarcastically that the Texas mob had 'vindicated the law' and that 'Southern civilization' had triumphed.
The New York Age printed the despatch inside an editorial comparing the scene to 'savages' and ending 'LET THE NATION WAKE UP!'

The Metropolis Weekly Gazette added 'Shame on so called christianed and civilized America!' to the Globe-Democrat report, and the Cleveland Gazette framed the AP item as 'Texas' and the south's answer'.
The Tulsa Star ran the AP account under '2 NEGROES ARE BURNED AT STAKE' without comment.
The Plaindealer's correspondent said the citizens 'roasted two Negroes' and stressed that no rape charge was made.
